name: Equal Rights Beyond Borders — Free Legal Aid for Refugees in Greece
description: Equal Rights Beyond Borders is a charitable organization founded in 2016, headquartered in Berlin and Athens, with offices on the Greek islands of Chios and Kos. The organization provides free legal aid and representation to more than 450 people on the move in Greece each year. Services include preparation for asylum interviews, accompaniment to hearings, submission of supporting memos, Dublin family reunification case assistance, and appeals against rejected asylum applications. In cases involving human rights violations, the organization applies for interim measures and lodges complaints before the European Court of Human Rights and the European Court of Justice. The majority of their clients are eventually released from detention, granted asylum or another form of protection in Greece, or reunited with their families in other EU countries. This is a critical resource for asylum seekers who arrive in Greece via Mediterranean routes and face complex legal proceedings with limited access to legal counsel.
eligibility: Asylum seekers, refugees, and displaced persons in Greece, including those on the Greek islands and mainland; no nationality restriction; services available regardless of immigration status or country of origin; priority given to individuals in administrative detention or facing deportation
amount: Free legal services — no direct financial grants; pro bono legal representation and case assistance provided at no cost
applicationProcess: Contact Equal Rights Beyond Borders through their website at equal-rights.org or visit their offices in Athens, Chios, or Kos. Referrals also accepted from UNHCR, other NGOs, and detention center staff. An intake assessment determines eligibility and urgency. Legal counselors will review your case and explain your options under Greek and EU asylum law. All services are provided free of charge in multiple languages including Arabic, Farsi, French, and English.
geographicScope: Greece — Athens (mainland), Chios island, Kos island, and cases before the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg
documentsRequired: Any identity documents available (passport, national ID, or UNHCR registration); asylum application documents if already filed; detention orders or deportation notices if applicable; medical records if relevant to the case. Documents are helpful but not required to receive initial legal consultation.

name: California Food Assistance Program (CFAP) — State Food Benefits for Immigrants
description: The California Food Assistance Program (CFAP) is a state-funded program that provides food benefits equivalent to the federal SNAP/CalFresh program to immigrants in California who are ineligible for federal food assistance due to their immigration status. Starting April 2026, as federal SNAP eligibility was further restricted for certain noncitizens under the 2025 reconciliation act, CFAP serves as a critical safety net ensuring that immigrants who lose federal benefits can continue to receive food assistance funded entirely by the state of California. CFAP provides the same monthly benefit amounts as CalFresh, loaded onto an EBT card that can be used at grocery stores, farmers markets, and authorized food retailers throughout California. The program covers lawful permanent residents who have not yet met the federal five-year residency requirement, refugees and asylees who have exceeded their federal eligibility period, and other qualified immigrants excluded from SNAP. California is one of the few states providing this level of state-funded food assistance to immigrant communities.
eligibility: California residents who are lawful immigrants ineligible for federal SNAP/CalFresh due to immigration status restrictions; includes lawful permanent residents who have not met the five-year residency requirement, refugees and asylees who have aged out of federal eligibility, and other legally present noncitizens; must meet CalFresh income and resource limits; must be a California resident
amount: Monthly food benefits — same amount as federal CalFresh/SNAP, varies by household size (e.g., approximately $234/month for a single person, up to $1,756/month for a family of 8 in 2026)
applicationProcess: Apply online at BenefitsCal.com, by phone at 1-877-847-3663, or in person at your county social services office. Complete the CalFresh application and indicate your immigration status. County workers will determine if you qualify for federal CalFresh or state-funded CFAP. Benefits are loaded monthly onto an EBT card. No Social Security number required for the applicant (only for household members who are applying for benefits). Processing time is typically 30 days, or 7 days for expedited cases with very low income.
documentsRequired: Proof of California residency (utility bill, lease, or mail with California address), proof of identity (any photo ID including foreign passport or consular ID), proof of income (pay stubs, employer letter, or self-attestation), proof of immigration status (visa, work permit, asylum approval, or green card); household composition information

name: SFILEN — San Francisco Immigrant Legal & Education Network
organization: San Francisco Immigrant Legal & Education Network (SFILEN)
description: The San Francisco Immigrant Legal & Education Network (SFILEN) is a collaborative network of legal service providers, community organizations, and pro bono attorneys coordinating free and low-cost immigration legal services throughout San Francisco. SFILEN connects immigrants and refugees with qualified legal representation for asylum cases, deportation defense, DACA renewals, family petitions, U-visas for crime victims, T-visas for trafficking survivors, and naturalization applications. The network also conducts know-your-rights workshops, legal clinics, and community education events in multiple languages including Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, and Arabic. SFILEN serves as a critical referral hub, ensuring that immigrants who cannot afford private attorneys are matched with appropriate legal providers based on their case type and language needs. The network is supported by the City and County of San Francisco and operates in partnership with the San Francisco Office of Civic Engagement and Immigrant Affairs.
eligibility: Immigrants, refugees, and asylum seekers residing in San Francisco regardless of immigration status; services available to undocumented individuals, DACA recipients, asylum seekers, refugees, visa holders, and lawful permanent residents; some services may have income eligibility requirements; priority given to low-income individuals who cannot afford private legal representation
amount: Free or low-cost immigration legal services — no direct financial grants; pro bono legal representation, legal consultations, and know-your-rights workshops provided at no cost through the network
applicationProcess: Visit the SFILEN website at sfilen.org to find legal service providers in your area, or call 311 (San Francisco city services) for a referral. Attend a free legal clinic or know-your-rights workshop. You will be screened for eligibility and matched with a legal provider based on your case type and language needs. Walk-in clinics are available at various community centers throughout San Francisco. Some providers accept cases by appointment.
geographicScope: San Francisco, California — city and county of San Francisco; some network partners also serve neighboring Bay Area counties
documentsRequired: Any identity documents available (passport, consular ID, or any photo ID); immigration documents if available (visa, work permit, prior applications); court notices or immigration hearing dates if applicable; proof of San Francisco residency (utility bill, lease, or mail); documents are helpful but not required for initial consultation

name: CARECEN SF — Central American Resource Center Legal & Social Services
description: The Central American Resource Center of San Francisco (CARECEN SF) is a nonprofit organization founded in 1985 that provides comprehensive immigration legal services, educational programs, and social services to the Latino and immigrant community in San Francisco's Mission District and beyond. CARECEN offers free and low-cost immigration legal consultations, help with asylum applications, TPS renewals, DACA applications, family-based petitions, naturalization assistance, and deportation defense. Beyond legal services, CARECEN provides ESL (English as a Second Language) classes, citizenship preparation courses, computer literacy training, youth leadership development programs, and community organizing support. The organization serves as a trusted community anchor for Central American and other Latin American immigrants, providing culturally and linguistically appropriate services in Spanish and English. CARECEN has helped thousands of immigrants navigate the U.S. immigration system, access social services, and integrate into their communities.
eligibility: Immigrants, refugees, and asylum seekers in the San Francisco Bay Area, with a focus on Central American and Latin American communities; services available regardless of immigration status — open to undocumented immigrants, TPS holders, DACA recipients, asylum seekers, and lawful permanent residents; low-income individuals prioritized for free legal services; ESL and education programs open to all
amount: Free or low-cost — immigration legal consultations, ESL classes, citizenship preparation, and social services provided at no or reduced cost; some services may have nominal fees on a sliding scale
applicationProcess: Call CARECEN at (415) 642-4400 to schedule a legal consultation, or visit their office in San Francisco's Mission District. Walk-in consultations are available during designated clinic hours. For ESL classes and citizenship preparation, register in person or by phone at the beginning of each session cycle. Intake staff will assess your legal needs and connect you with the appropriate service. All services are available in Spanish and English.
geographicScope: San Francisco Bay Area, California — primary office in San Francisco's Mission District; serves clients from across the Bay Area
documentsRequired: Any identity documents available (passport, consular ID, matrícula consular, or any photo ID); immigration documents if available (visa, I-94, prior USCIS notices, TPS documentation, DACA approval); court notices or deportation orders if applicable; proof of address in the Bay Area

name: I Have Rights — Free Legal Aid for Refugees on Lesvos, Greece
description: I Have Rights is a grassroots legal aid organization operating on the island of Lesvos, Greece, one of the primary arrival points for refugees and asylum seekers crossing the Aegean Sea from Turkey. The organization provides free legal assistance to asylum seekers housed in the Reception and Identification Centre on Lesvos, covering all stages of the asylum procedure including initial registration, asylum interview preparation, appeals against negative decisions, and family reunification under the Dublin Regulation. I Have Rights also documents and advocates against human rights violations at EU external borders, including pushbacks and conditions of detention. Their legal team includes qualified lawyers and trained legal volunteers who provide services in multiple languages including Arabic, Farsi, French, Somali, and English. The organization plays a critical role in ensuring access to justice for some of the most vulnerable people arriving in Europe, many of whom have no other access to legal representation on the islands.
eligibility: Asylum seekers and refugees on the island of Lesvos, Greece; no nationality or documentation requirement; services available to all individuals in the asylum procedure regardless of country of origin; priority given to vulnerable individuals including unaccompanied minors, survivors of torture, and persons with urgent legal deadlines
amount: Free legal services — no direct financial grants; pro bono legal representation, asylum interview preparation, and human rights documentation provided at no cost
applicationProcess: Visit the I Have Rights office on Lesvos or contact the organization through their website at ihaverights.eu. Referrals are also accepted from UNHCR, camp management, and other NGOs operating on Lesvos. Legal counselors conduct an intake assessment to understand your case and timeline. Services include one-on-one legal consultations, interview preparation sessions, and full legal representation for appeals. All services are free and available in Arabic, Farsi, French, Somali, and English.
geographicScope: Lesvos, Greece — primarily serves asylum seekers in the Lesvos Reception and Identification Centre; legal cases may proceed to courts in Athens and the European Court of Human Rights
documentsRequired: Any identity documents available (passport, national ID, or UNHCR registration card); asylum registration documents if already in the procedure; any correspondence from Greek asylum authorities; medical records or evidence of persecution if available. Initial legal consultation does not require documents.

name: Switchboard Settle In — Multilingual Resource Hub for Newcomers to the United States
description: Switchboard is a federally funded technical assistance program operated by the International Rescue Committee (IRC) that provides a comprehensive, free resource hub for refugee service providers and newcomers in the United States. Through its Settle In platform, Switchboard offers trusted, culturally appropriate information in more than 10 languages to help refugees, asylees, and other newcomers navigate life in the United States. Topics covered include finding housing, accessing healthcare, enrolling children in school, understanding workers' rights, obtaining a driver's license, opening a bank account, accessing food assistance, learning English, and understanding the U.S. legal system. The Switchboard Community Support Line provides direct referrals to local service providers. For service providers, Switchboard offers training webinars, toolkits, and research on best practices in refugee resettlement. This is a critical first-stop resource for any newcomer trying to understand what services are available and how to access them in their community.
eligibility: Refugees, asylees, Special Immigrant Visa (SIV) holders, Cuban/Haitian entrants, trafficking survivors, and other ORR-eligible newcomers to the United States; Settle In information resources are freely accessible to anyone regardless of immigration status; Community Support Line available to newcomers and service providers nationwide
amount: Free information and referral services — no direct financial grants; multilingual resource guides, webinars, and the Community Support Line provided at no cost
applicationProcess: Access the Settle In platform at settlein.org for multilingual information on housing, healthcare, education, employment, and more. Contact the Switchboard Community Support Line for personalized referrals to local service providers in your area. No registration or application is required to access information. Resources are available in Arabic, Burmese, Dari, Farsi, French, Kinyarwanda, Pashto, Somali, Spanish, Swahili, Ukrainian, and English.
geographicScope: United States — nationwide; Settle In provides general information applicable across all states, with local referrals available through the Community Support Line
documentsRequired: None required — information resources are freely accessible to anyone. For referrals to specific local service providers, having your location (city or zip code) helps the Community Support Line connect you with nearby resources.
